title: NAM 'Selling Free Enterprise' Campaign Begins: 15-Year Business Assault on Labor and Liberalism
description: The National Association of Manufacturers (NAM), along with the Committee for Economic Development and other business organizations, launches a comprehensive 15-year campaign (1945-1960) to discredit New Deal liberalism and undermine the power and legitimacy of organized labor, as documented by historian Elizabeth Fones-Wolf in 'Selling Free Enterprise: The Business Assault on Labor and Liberalism, 1945-60.' Conservative business leaders strive to reorient workers away from loyalties to organized labor and government, teaching that prosperity comes through individual initiative, increased productivity, and protection of personal liberty. This 'ideological and propagandistic civil war' is waged on the shop floor, in public schools and universities, churches, local communities, state and federal legislatures, and through radio, television, movie theaters, and print media. Business groups permeate 'every aspect of American life, including factories, schools, churches, and community institutions.' NAM deploys sustained visual propaganda in workplaces and public spaces, informed by the belief that habitual exposure to emotion-laden messaging has a 'constructive effect' on viewers' dispositions. By 1960, New Deal collectivist ideology emphasizing social justice and wealth redistribution is replaced by individualistic ideology associating freedom with productivity, individualism, and unregulated business. Major victories include Taft-Hartley Act (1947) and Landrum-Griffin Act (1959).

sources.title: Selling Free Enterprise: The Business Assault on Labor and Liberalism, 1945-60
The National Association of Manufacturers and Visual Propaganda

significance: Demonstrates comprehensive corporate strategy to reshape American political culture across all major institutions simultaneously—factories, schools, churches, media, government. The 15-year campaign's success in replacing New Deal collectivism with free-market individualism shows effectiveness of sustained, coordinated propaganda. NAM's penetration of schools (economic education), churches (linking capitalism to Christianity), and media (Industry on Parade, print advertising) creates multi-generational ideological shift. This campaign predates Powell Memo by 26 years, showing corporate ideological infrastructure already sophisticated and effective. Fones-Wolf's research demonstrates Powell Memo didn't create corporate political mobilization—it built on decades of existing infrastructure.
